title: Datlantis pitches underwater data centers powered by offshore wind
html:
An underwater data center startup from Sweden says it wants to connect servers to offshore wind turbines.

Datlantis has carried out first tests of its data center module, and says it is gearing up for a pilot scheme.

It is the latest company to try its hand at offshore data centers, and news of the trial comes at the same time as Russian hosting provider RuVDS revealed it is testing a floating platform for compute.

The men from Datlantis

Datlantis said it has tested “underwater data center prototypes that can be deployed and recovered on-demand in just a few minutes.” It did not disclose where the trial took place, or whether any compute was on board. It posted a video of the test on LinkedIn, which features a cameo from an inquisitive jellyfish.

Writing on LinkedIn, the company’s CEO Miguel Marques said: "We validated our high-density cooling system and flexible maintenance operations in a real environment, even under changing currents and tides.

“We also looked at the environmental impact of our data center, analyzing its thermal impact on surrounding waters and how our operations interact with marine life.

“These tests were the culmination of months of hard work from our team, and we're now preparing for our first pilot coming soon, where we're offering high-density IT infrastructure in several locations across Europe.”

According to its website, Stockholm-based Datlantis intends to pair its data centers with offshore wind installations. It says it will maintain the data centers using robots, and that it intends to harness the cold ocean temperatures to cool its servers.

Marques is a marine engineer with a background in offshore wind.

Companies including Aikido and Exascale Labs have also proposed offshore wind-powered data centers, while HiCloud claims to have an operational underwater unit attached to a turbine off the coast of China.

From Russia to the Antarctic

Up on the ocean surface, RuVDS has announced it is testing a floating data center to support a scientific mission to Antarctica.

According to a report from Tass, the floating data center will be used as part of a mission by Russian scientists to scale Mount Siple in the Antarctic.

It will be used to process telemetry and weather data, analyze drone data, and provide communications services for the explorers. Mount Siple, which stands at some 3,100 meters (10,300 feet) has never been climbed successfully before.

In a statement to Tass, RuVDS said: “The RuVDS hosting provider will deploy a floating data center aboard an expedition vessel in Antarctica. Access to the equipment operating directly on board will be available to anyone.

“The computing power of several servers will support the simultaneous operation of hundreds of virtual machines, simultaneously covering the workload of the scientists who will use the equipment as part of the expedition. The key event of the scientific mission will be the first-ever ascent of Mount Siple, one of the last unclimbed peaks on the planet.”

RuVDS CEO Nikita Tsaplin added that the voyage will also be a test of how the servers perform in potentially hazardous ocean conditions. The party is due to set off in January, with the mission concluding in March.
summary: Elsewhere, Russia prepares to send floating data center to the Antarctic
